title: 403 long option trades, 15% win rate. Posting because I only ever see the winning screenshots
author: QuanTradin
selftext:
Paper, real quotes, month of it. Long option side came out at 15% wins across 403 trades, −$300,517.

Same window, shares instead: 47% wins, −$56,578 across 2,095 trades. Nearly flat.

Same signals in a lot of cases. The wrapper was the entire difference and it cost about six times more than everything else combined.

Worst single trade was −$20,330. Average loser overall is −$384 against an average winner of +$189, so I'm losing two dollars for every one I make and winning less than half the time. Bad combination.

Genuinely asking, does anyone here run a long premium book that clears its costs over a few thousand trades? Every time I work through the maths you need direction and timing and size of move all right, and I keep missing at least one.

comments.author: Strong_Chard_4353
comments.body:
Respect for actually posting the real numbers. This is the kind of transparency the trading community needs more of honestly. Everyone posts their winners and hides the rest.

  
The direction + timing + size of move problem you mentioned is exactly what got me thinking about signal quality over trade quantity. I've been working on a project called InsiderPulse (https://insiderpulse.org) that tries to tackle that from a different angle. Instead of executing trades, it uses AI to score and flag market signals so you can focus on the setups that actually have edge rather than spreading across hundreds of trades.

  
Curious what your bot uses for entry signals though. That 42% win rate on the share side vs 15% on options tells a pretty interesting story about how much the instrument wrapper matters.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body:
Reasonable, and our own numbers argue your side rather than mine. That post was 403 long option trades at a 15% win rate — buying premium and being wrong most of the time is precisely the failure mode you're avoiding.

The honest complication is that I can't yet grade your side as well as I grade mine, and I'd rather say so than show you a flattering number.

The credit structures — put-writes, put-spreads, iron condors — are priced by a Black-Scholes model in the backtest rather than off the real chain. Every one of those results is stamped BSMODEL and carries a disclosure, because the model flatters: our own iron condor read +13.6% in the modelled backtest and then ran -5.9% a week at real prices. Same structure, and essentially all of that difference is the bid-ask you actually pay, which a theoretical mid never charges you. Multi-leg flatters worst, because you pay it on every leg.

So if you tested a short-premium strategy on it today, the number would be too kind — and the product says that in those words on the result rather than letting you discover it live.

The long side prices off the real chain instead: nearest real contract to a target expiry and moneyness, asking for a measured two-sided quote and reporting what share of the fills actually got one. Getting the short-premium path to that standard is the work I'd have to finish before I'd claim anything to someone who only sells.

One other thing worth saying to you specifically: early assignment isn't simulated. Short legs are carried to expiry and settled there, which is the favourable case for a seller. It's disclosed at deploy time, but it's the assumption I'd want you to know about before you trusted any short-premium result of mine.
